newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Chiluba, MMD head for decisive victory.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Chiluba, MMD head for decisive victory.

text.p: Zambian President Frederick Chiluba and his ruling party headed for a decisive victory on Wednesday in the southern African country's disputed election, which was marked by an opposition boycott and a low turnout.

Chiluba led the presidential race with over 60 percent of the vote while his Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD) secured at least 108 of the 150 seats in parliament, partial results from the elections office showed.
Opposition parties contesting Monday's polls had won 19 out of the 127 seats for which final results had been compiled, the office said.
"The complete results will be known by Thursday morning," Joel Sikawe, acting director of elections, told Reuters.
Chiluba is expected to be inaugurated for a second term as president on Thursday, after the final results are announced.

He was leading with 600,965 of the 786,583 votes counted by mid-afternoon -- enough to give him at least 50 percent of the estimated 1.1 million votes cast overall, even before results from 63 remaining constituencies were counted.
Election monitors based their forecast of the total turnout on the number of voters who both registered and collected their voting cards, signalling intention to vote.

Political analysts and opposition figures said that while Chiluba was sure of re-election, his victory would be marred by the low turnout, which was partly due to the opposition's call for a boycott of the election.
Chiluba's closest rival, Zambia Democratic Congress leader Dean Mungomba, who has run a distant second in the poll, said there was a risk of outbreaks of violence following the vote.
Speaking to reporters, he advised foreigners living in Zambia to leave.
"We are merely asking them to take cover because our next course of action is not likely to be peaceful," Mungomba said.
Dozens of his supporters marched through the capital Lusaka on Wednesday to protest against the results giving Chiluba a landslide victory. Police broke up the rally and there were no arrests.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the poll, charging that Chiluba had rigged the campaign in advance and said they would not recognise the result.

Former president Kenneth Kaunda, who ruled from independence in 1964 until Chiluba trounced him in Zambia's first free polls in 1991, was barred from contesting the poll by a new law because his parents, from Malawi, were not Zambian.
Kaunda led the opposition boycott of the campaign and called for economic sanctions on Zambia.

The Committee for a Clean Campaign, a Zambian umbrella group of 19 non-governmental and civic groups which monitored the ballot, said that while the voting itself had been correct, the run-up to the election gave the ruling party an unfair advantage.

The committee said that flawed voter registration, abuses of government resources and partisan state-run media had favoured Chiluba's MMD. Half of Zambia's 4.6 million eligible voters were excluded from the rolls because of flawed registration.
"In view of all this, the 1996 presidential and parliamentary elections cannot be said to have been free and fair," the statement said.

An international observer group, which included monitors from several southern African states as well as Canada, Denmark, Sweden, Australia and Germany, said, however, the poll was "generally free and fair".
"The process was good and transparent, and we have not detected any evidence of foul play," said a statement by the monitoring group, working under the auspices of the Christian Council of Zambia.
